evidence.claim: A lift bridge and mine shafthouses mark the road to Copper Harbor.
evidence.quote: The highway continues up Quincy Hill and out of town, passing the Quincy Mine at the top of the hill.

evidence.claim: A lift bridge
evidence.quote: The Portage Lake Lift Bridge (officially the Houghton–Hancock Bridge) connects the cities of Hancock and Houghton

evidence.claim: mine shafthouses
evidence.quote: historic downtowns, mine shafthouses

evidence.claim: the road to Copper Harbor.
evidence.quote: The two highways meet one last time in Copper Harbor

evidence.claim: US 41 climbs Quincy Hill above Hancock before following the center of the Keweenaw Peninsula through Calumet toward Phoenix.
evidence.quote: The highway continues up Quincy Hill and out of town, passing the Quincy Mine at the top of the hill.

evidence.claim: US 41 climbs Quincy Hill above Hancock before following the center of the Keweenaw Peninsula through Calumet toward Phoenix.
evidence.quote: US 41 merges with M-26 in Calumet, and they follow the center of the Keweenaw Peninsula to the community of Phoenix.

evidence.claim: The Copper Country Trail organization presents this National Byway as a journey through mining history and the peninsula’s natural features.
evidence.quote: Attractions abound along the Copper Country Trail National Byway. From Hancock and Houghton to Calumet through Copper Harbor, you will be immersed in Upper Michigan’s rich mining history , picturesque landscape , and natural features.

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration’s archived description gives 47 miles and an hour for a one-way drive, with historic downtowns and mine shafthouses carrying the story.
evidence.quote: Length 47.0 mi / 75.6 km Time to Allow Take 60 minutes to drive the byway one-way

evidence.claim: with historic downtowns and mine shafthouses carrying the story.
evidence.quote: Today, the story of the Copper Country is told in the historic downtowns, mine shafthouses, and through the history of the people.

evidence.claim: Congress authorized a military wagon road in 1863, providing a land connection when ice or storms stopped Great Lakes transport.
evidence.quote: The road was also needed during the five or six months of the year that transportation on the Great Lakes was barred by ice or stormy weather.

evidence.claim: Congress authorized a military wagon road in 1863
evidence.quote: Congress passed a law to build a military wagon road on March 3, 1863

evidence.claim: The 1864 layout followed today’s US 41 between Houghton and Phoenix, then today’s M-26 toward Copper Harbor.
evidence.quote: The road was laid out in 1864 following what is today M-26 between Copper Harbor and Phoenix, US 41 south to Houghton

evidence.claim: The wagon road was poorly built and barely passable except when the ground froze or snow covered it; nearby railroads attracted more traffic.
evidence.quote: Railroads built near the Military Road attracted more traffic than the road. The road was not well built; except in the winter when the weather froze the ground or covered it in snow, the road was barely passable.

evidence.claim: US 41 received its number in 1926; national byway designation followed in 2005.
evidence.quote: US 41 was first designated as a US Highway in 1926.

evidence.claim: national byway designation followed in 2005.
evidence.quote: On September 22, 2005, US 41 north of Houghton was designated the Copper Country Trail of the National Scenic Byways program.

evidence.claim: Begin in Houghton, cross the Portage Lake Lift Bridge to Hancock and climb past Quincy Mine.
evidence.quote: The two streets merge west of downtown at the southern end of the Portage Lake Lift Bridge.

evidence.claim: to Hancock and climb past Quincy Mine.
evidence.quote: North of the lift bridge, US 41 turns west through the downtown of Hancock

evidence.claim: Continue through Calumet to Phoenix, where US 41 turns east through Central and Delaware.
evidence.quote: US 41 merges with M-26 in Calumet, and they follow the center of the Keweenaw Peninsula to the community of Phoenix. M-26 turns northwesterly in Phoenix to loop through Eagle River and Eagle Harbor, while US 41 turns easterly through the rural communities of Central and Delaware.

evidence.claim: At Copper Harbor, Brockway Mountain Drive is a separate loop off M-26, with twists, hills and sharp hairpins.
evidence.quote: The road can be accessed from either Eagle Harbor or Copper Harbor and serves as a scenic loop off M-26.

evidence.claim: with twists, hills and sharp hairpins.
evidence.quote: The roadway twists and turns as it alternately climbs and descends several smaller hills along the ridgeline.

evidence.claim: sharp hairpins.
evidence.quote: Near the eastern end, there are two sharp hairpin turns

evidence.claim: US 41 itself continues past Fort Wilkins State Park to a cul-de-sac marked by a wooden sign.
evidence.quote: Past the park entrance, US 41 ends at a cul-de-sac, marked by a large wooden sign.

evidence.claim: The bridge between Houghton and Hancock was designed to carry both roads and rails on its movable span.
evidence.quote: The original 1959 design by Hazelet and Erdal of Chicago of the bridge's liftspan had roadways constructed on both levels with rails embedded in the road surface on the lower deck.

evidence.claim: Partly raising the span let smaller boats pass underneath without stopping vehicles; trains required the span to be lowered.
evidence.quote: This allowed the span to be partially raised to allow small and medium boat traffic to pass underneath without disrupting vehicular traffic. From this middle position, the span would then only need to be raised for large ships or lowered to allow trains to cross.

evidence.claim: The present bridge replaced a swing bridge in 1959.
evidence.quote: In 1959, the Portage Canal Swing Bridge was replaced

evidence.claim: Rail service ended in 1982, changing how the two decks were used.
evidence.quote: With the end of rail service in 1982, the lowest position is no longer needed to allow trains to pass

evidence.claim: In winter, after the lake freezes, the span is lowered so snowmobiles can use the bottom deck.
evidence.quote: In the winter after the lake freezes, the bridge is placed in the lowest position to allow the lower deck to be used by snowmobile traffic.

evidence.claim: The crossing is the only land link between the northern and southern sections of the Keweenaw Peninsula.
evidence.quote: It is the only land-based link between the north (so-called Copper Island) and south sections of the Keweenaw peninsula.

evidence.claim: Quincy’s No. 2 shaft followed the copper deposit for 9,260 feet on a 55-degree slope, reaching 6,200 feet vertically below its entrance.
evidence.quote: at 9,260 feet (2.82 km or 1.75 miles) along the dip of the deposit on a 55 degree decline. (measured vertically from the shaft collar, the depth is 6,200 feet.)

evidence.claim: A steam hoist built in 1918 raised and lowered ore and workers along that shaft.
evidence.quote: To raise and lower ore and workers into this shaft, the world's largest steam-driven mine hoist was built in 1918

evidence.claim: Its elaborate hoist house served as a showpiece for visiting investors.
evidence.quote: The very decorative Hoist House was used as a showpiece for visiting investors.

evidence.claim: Despite the investment, the steam hoist was used for only eleven years, ending in 1929.
evidence.quote: but was used for only eleven years until it ceased usage in 1929.

evidence.claim: Since mining stopped, groundwater has filled the workings up to the seventh level.
evidence.quote: The shafts and stopes of the Quincy Mine have slowly filled with groundwater since the closing of the mine. The water has currently filled the mine up to the seventh level

evidence.claim: A drainage tunnel keeps that level clear; Michigan Tech enlarged the tunnel in the 1970s for a mining study.
evidence.quote: The seventh level is drained by a large adit

evidence.claim: Michigan Tech enlarged the tunnel in the 1970s for a mining study.
evidence.quote: was enlarged by Michigan Tech in the 1970s for a mining study.

evidence.claim: Low stone walls line Brockway Mountain Drive as it climbs the Keweenaw Fault’s ridge above Lake Superior.
evidence.quote: Brockway Mountain Drive ascends along the ridgeline of the Keweenaw Fault.

evidence.claim: Low stone walls line Brockway Mountain Drive
evidence.quote: The drive is lined with low stone walls

evidence.claim: The county road commission began construction in 1933 with federal funding to employ copper miners left jobless by the Depression.
evidence.quote: Construction of Brockway Mountain Drive began in early 1933 by the Keweenaw County Road Commission with federal highway funding designed to provide meaningful work to the many copper miners who became unemployed during the Great Depression.

evidence.claim: Workers graded the road by hand, assisted by horses.
evidence.quote: The work required to build the road was carried out by manual labor, with the assistance of a team of horses

evidence.claim: The road opened in October 1933, with work on its stone walls continuing the following year.
evidence.quote: The road was opened for public use that October 14

evidence.claim: with work on its stone walls continuing the following year.
evidence.quote: During 1934, additional work was done to the roadway to build the stone walls.

evidence.claim: The route reaches 720 feet above the lake, with viewpoints over Copper Harbor, Lake Superior and undeveloped woodland.
evidence.quote: 720 feet (219 m) above the surface of Lake Superior. Several viewpoints along the route allow for panoramas of Copper Harbor, Lake Superior, and undeveloped woodland.

evidence.claim: Toward Copper Harbor, two sharp hairpins lead into the descent from the ridge.
evidence.quote: Near the eastern end, there are two sharp hairpin turns

evidence.claim: Toward Copper Harbor, two sharp hairpins lead into the descent from the ridge.
evidence.quote: the road makes its steep descent down from the ridge, through the second turn and ends at M-26 on the western edge of town.

evidence.claim: Brockway Mountain Drive is not plowed and is closed to cars in winter, when it serves as a snowmobile trail.
evidence.quote: During the winter, Brockway Mountain Drive is closed to cars as the Keweenaw County Road Commission does not plow the road; instead the drive is used as a snowmobile trail.

flags: Cached Michigan DOT driving guide contains only an archive wrapper, not the guide. Its catalog claims were not used.

Bridge pages disagree on clearance and predecessor dates. Omitted those measurements and dates, and the unqualified current superlative.
Brockway construction began and the road first opened in 1933; further work continued afterward. The current single-year wording was narrowed.
